facts.statement: The holotype skeleton of Rebbachisaurus was discovered in 1948 in the Errachidia Province of Morocco.
facts.quote: The skeleton, discovered in 1948, was unearthed in the Errachidia Province of Morocco from strata of the Kem Kem Beds.

facts.statement: French paleontologist René Lavocat discovered fossils of Rebbachisaurus between October 1948 and April 1949 at the Gara Sbaa locality in Morocco.
facts.quote: Fossils assigned to Rebbachisaurus were first discovered in the Gara Sbaa locality in Errachidia Province, southeastern Morocco between 8 October 1948 and 1 April 1949 by French paleontologist René Lavocat.

facts.statement: René Lavocat formally described and named the species Rebbachisaurus garasbae in 1954.
facts.quote: In 1954, Lavocat scientifically described the remains and assigned them to a new genus and species of sauropod, which he named Rebbachisaurus garasbae.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was deposited at the National Museum of Natural History in Paris under the number MNHN-MRS 1958 by January 1952.
facts.quote: By 3 January 1952, the last of the four expeditions to recover the fossils had concluded and the specimen was then brought to the National Museum of Natural History in Paris where it was deposited under specimen number MNHN-MRS 1958.

facts.statement: Rebbachisaurus lived in Africa during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 99 to 97 million years ago.
facts.quote: Rebbachisaurus (meaning "Aït Rebbach lizard") is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived in what is now Africa during the Late Cretaceous period, between 99 and 97 million years ago.

facts.statement: Much of the anatomy of Rebbachisaurus garasbae remains unknown because it is known only from a single incomplete skeleton.
facts.quote: Known from a single, incomplete skeleton, much of R. garasbae's anatomy is unknown.

facts.statement: Recent estimates suggest Rebbachisaurus was about 14 meters long and weighed between 7 and 12 metric tons.
facts.quote: Although once thought to be as long as 20 m in length, more recent estimates place it at 14 m long and weighing 7 - 12 MT.

facts.statement: Rebbachisaurus vertebrae could reach up to 150 cm in height, which is significantly taller than those of South American rebbachisaurids.
facts.quote: Its vertebrae are very tall and reach up to 150 cm tall, while those of South American rebbachisaurids get to only around 50 cm.

facts.statement: Rebbachisaurus garasbae is the only currently valid species within the genus Rebbachisaurus.
facts.quote: The only valid species is R. garasbae.

facts.statement: Some researchers have hypothesized that R. tamesnensis is a camarasaurid rather than a diplodocoid or valid species.
facts.quote: In 1995, Argentine paleontologists Jorge Calvo and Leonardo Salgado stated that R. tamesnensis was not a species or even a diplodocoid, but instead a camarasaurid based on its spatulate teeth, distally expanded ischium, and the presence of a hyposphene-hypantrum in the dorsal vertebrae.

facts.statement: It has been hypothesized that R. tamesnensis is a chimera composed of fossils from Jobaria and Nigersaurus.
facts.quote: However, in 2009 British paleontologist Philip D. Mannion hypothesized that R. tamesnensis was actually a chimera (a species named based on fossils of several different species) of Jobaria and Nigersaurus fossils, which was supported by other studies.

facts.statement: In 2004, Salgado and colleagues reclassified R. tessonei as a separate genus named Limaysaurus.
facts.quote: However, in 2004 Salgado and colleagues placed R. tessonei in its own genus, Limaysaurus.

facts.statement: Rebbachisaurus is classified as a medium-sized sauropod but represents one of the largest known rebbachisaurids.
facts.quote: Rebbachisaurus is a medium-sized sauropod, though it is among the largest rebbachisaurids known.

facts.statement: Recent studies estimate Rebbachisaurus was approximately 14 meters long and weighed between 7 and 12 metric tons.
facts.quote: Recent studies state that Rebbachisaurus was around 14 m long and weighed 7 - 12 MT.

facts.statement: Only one dorsal vertebra from the holotype specimen is relatively complete.
facts.quote: Only one dorsal vertebra from the holotype is relatively complete.

facts.statement: The estimated total height of Rebbachisaurus is 145 centimeters, though this estimate accounts for the missing distal 5% of the specimen.
facts.quote: Its estimated total height is 145 cm, as it is missing the distal most 5% of its length.

facts.statement: Rebbachisaurus is significantly taller than South American rebbachisaurids, which are only about 50 centimeters in height.
facts.quote: This makes it significantly taller than those observed in South American rebbachisaurids, which are only around 50 cm in height.

facts.statement: Rebbachisaurus is unique among sauropods because the infrazygapophyseal region of its neural arch is roughly the same height as the centrum.
facts.quote: Rebbachisaurus is unique amongst sauropods in that the infrazygapophyseal region of the neural arch is subequal in height to the centrum.

facts.statement: Although not fully preserved, the humerus of Rebbachisaurus is estimated to be between 100 and 105 centimeters in complete length.
facts.quote: The humerus is not fully preserved, but was estimated to be around 100-105 cm in complete length.

facts.statement: Most pelvic material from the MNHN collection is missing, except for a preserved fragment of the right ischium.
facts.quote: Most of the pelvic material has been missing from the MNHN, though there is a fragment of the right ischium preserved.

facts.statement: Wilson and Allain (2015) identified three sacral neural spines as spines 1–3, but this identification was based solely on comparisons with Nigersaurus.
facts.quote: Wilson and Allain (2015) stated they were sacral spines 1–3, though this was only based on comparisons with Nigersaurus.

facts.statement: Rebbachisaurus serves as the type genus for the family Rebbachisauridae and the subfamily Rebbachisaurinae.
facts.quote: Rebbachisaurus is the type genus of the family Rebbachisauridae and subfamily Rebbachisaurinae.

facts.statement: Rebbachisaurus was the first rebbachisaurid dinosaur to be discovered and named.
facts.quote: Rebbachisaurus was the first rebbachisaurid to be discovered or named.

facts.statement: Before its classification as a diplocodoid rebbachisaurid, Rebbachisaurus was assigned to the families Camarasauridae and Haplocanthosauridae.
facts.quote: Prior to being recognized as a diplocodoid rebbachisaurid, Rebbachisaurus was placed in the families Camarasauridae and Haplocanthosauridae

facts.statement: The family Rebbachisauridae was established by Bonaparte in 1997.
facts.quote: Rebbachisauridae was a clade created by Bonaparte (1997)

facts.statement: Salgado and colleagues defined Rebbachisauridae in 2004 as the group of diplodocoids more closely related to Rebbachisaurus than to Diplodocus.
facts.quote: This family was then defined as the clade as all diplodocoids more closely related to Rebbachisaurus than Diplodocus by Salgado and colleagues (2004).

facts.statement: Wilson and Allain first used the name Rebbachisaurinae in 2015.
facts.quote: The name Rebbachisaurinae was first used by Wilson and Allain (2015)

facts.statement: Wilson and Allain hypothesized in 2015 that Rebbachisauridae consisted of two geographic clades: the South American Limaysaurinae and the Euro-African Nigersaurinae.
facts.quote: Studies like Wilson and Allain (2015) have hypothesized that Rebbachisauridae was divided into two geographic clades: Limaysaurinae, a South American clade, and Nigersaurinae, a Euro-African clade.

facts.statement: Mannion and colleagues noted in 2019 that Nigersaurus might not belong in the Rebbachisaurinae clade because it is the sister taxon to other nigersaurines.
facts.quote: Mannion and colleagues (2019) pointed out that since Nigersaurus was found to be the sister taxon of all other nigersaurines in some studies, a Rebbachisaurinae clade may not necessarily include Nigersaurus itself

facts.statement: Fanti and colleagues created the group Khebbashia in 2015 to include Rebbachisaurus, Nigersaurus, and Limaysaurus.
facts.quote: In 2015, Fanti and colleagues erected Khebbashia, a group including Limaysaurinae and Rebbachisaurinae, as the least inclusive group including Rebbachisaurus, Nigersaurus, and Limaysaurus.

facts.statement: Simón and Salgado found in 2025 that the subfamilies Limaysaurinae, Nigersaurinae, and Rebbachisaurinae do not represent valid clades.
facts.quote: Additionally, in their 2025 description of the rebbachisaurid Cienciargentina, María Edith Simón and Salgado did not find Limaysaurinae, Nigersaurinae, or Rebbachisaurinae to be clades

facts.statement: Lucas Lerzo and colleagues recovered Rebbachisaurinae and Nigersaurinae as separate clades in 2024.
facts.quote: In contrast, Lucas Lerzo and colleagues (2024) recovered Rebbachisaurinae and Nigersaurinae as separate clades.

facts.statement: Ibiricu and colleagues suggested in 2017 that postcranial skeletal pneumaticity in rebbachisaurids was an adaptation to lower skeletal density.
facts.quote: In 2017, the Argentinian palaeontologist Lucio M. Ibiricu and colleagues examined the postcranial skeletal pneumaticity in the skeletons of rebbachisaurids, and suggested that it was an adaptation for lowering the density of the skeleton

facts.statement: John Whitlock studied dental microwear on a tooth assigned to Rebbachisaurus in 2011.
facts.quote: In a 2011 study, American paleontologist John Whitlock studied the dental microwear of a tooth assigned to Rebbachisaurus

facts.statement: Traits of its teeth suggest that Rebbachisaurus was a generalist ground-height browser.
facts.quote: These two traits suggest that it was a generalist ground-height browser.

facts.statement: Ibrahim and colleagues suggested in 2020 that Rebbachisaurus likely lacked the self-supporting tooth rows found in Nigersaurus based on wear patterns.
facts.quote: Based on a tooth possibly coming from Rebbachisaurus, Ibrahim and colleagues (2020) noted differences in wear patterns between Nigersaurus and an isolated tooth that may indicate that Rebbachisaurus lacked the derived, self-supporting tooth rows found in Nigersaurus.
